exhibits.title: LOCIT
exhibits.category: Engineering · Product Development · Hardware and Software
exhibits.teaser: A smart location-tracking necklace with a companion app for live location and safety alerts.

image.alt: Three phone screens from the LOCIT companion app: a teal sign-in screen, a campus map with a location pin, and a geofence screen with an out-of-bounds warning.

idea.text: A smart location-tracking necklace paired with a phone app. It tracks GPS location, watches a geofence and monitors temperature.

who.text: Families with young children or elderly relatives who want to locate a loved one in real time, without the wearer needing to carry a phone.

how.text: The necklace uploads sensor data to a web server, which processes and stores it. The app fetches that data to show live location and send boundary, temperature and low-battery alerts.

items.text: Families need an easy way to find young children and elderly relatives in real time. The leading trackers, Apple AirTag and Tile, depend on a phone, which the people LOCIT was meant for often don’t carry.
LOCIT was designed to improve personal safety by tracking the wearer’s location and alerting when they cross a set boundary.
The goal was peace of mind: a lightweight, rechargeable tracker that works on its own, with safe-zone alerts when the wearer wanders too far.
I led a four-person engineering team from design through testing.
I wrote the product requirements document, with measurable targets such as 24-hour battery life and geofencing alert accuracy, and tested the prototype against them.
Scope: GPS tracking, geofencing, sensors and actuators, safety alerts, application development, requirements gathering, team coordination and system testing.
I designed the team’s AZAD logo.
I demoed the system to non-technical audiences.

figures.alt: AZAD team logo: a winged emblem with a power-button icon and a signal-green accent above the word AZAD.
figures.caption: AZAD, the LOCIT team mark I designed.

items.text: The first 3D-printed enclosure was too bulky to wear comfortably as a necklace, so it was reduced in size and iterated until the GPS module, microcontroller and battery fit.
FlutterFlow could not handle the real-time data coming from AWS.
Hard targets for a wearable: under 15 grams, location within 3 feet, updates every 30 seconds, and up to three trackers per phone.

figures.alt: Hand sketch of the LOCIT necklace pendant: a round case on a cord, with the circuit board, wiring and modules drawn inside it in red.
figures.caption: Early concept sketch: what had to fit inside the pendant.

items.text: Market: the PRD cites nearly half a billion smart wearables sold worldwide in 2023 (Statista) and describes a fragmented market led by Apple AirTag and Tile, both of which need a phone.
Form factor: compared a necklace pendant, an armband, a pin or brooch, and a sling bag for comfort, discretion and keeping a camera facing forward. The team chose the pendant.
Moved data handling out of the app and onto a web server: the necklace uploads sensor data, the server processes and stores it, and the app fetches it.
Refined the geofencing algorithms and accuracy thresholds, because GPS accuracy affected how precisely boundary crossings were detected.
Cut scope to fit the prototype: ultraviolet sensors were dropped because of long procurement lead times, Bluetooth was added, and the requirements were revised to match what was built.

Companion app built in FlutterFlow: home, settings and profile pages, a five-icon bottom navigation bar, and a Google Maps widget meant to connect to the necklace’s GPS. The UI was planned in Figma with a site map and a first design draft.
App features: real-time GPS location, geofencing with boundary-crossing notifications, a temperature alert when the device gets too hot, and a battery alert below 20%.
Necklace enclosure designed in Autodesk Fusion 360 and 3D-printed in PLA, with iterations tested for component fit.
Facial recognition was specified as a requirement and designed into the app screens. Whether it worked in the final prototype is not confirmed here.
items.src: Product requirements document; app design screens

figures.caption: Enclosure modeled in Fusion 360.

figures.caption: App design screens: sign in, geofencing, settings.

items.text: Tested GPS tracking and geofencing alerts across 20+ scenarios: 98% location accuracy and 100% alert accuracy.
About 20% faster sensor data transfer after replacing the direct AWS integration with a web server, giving faster GPS updates and geofencing alerts.

results.needs: The test data behind these numbers.

items.text: Next steps listed at the time: at least 24 hours of battery life on one charge, thorough testing, UI refinement and user testing. These were plans, not results.
Nice-to-haves left for later: two-way voice with the wearer, a low-battery mode that keeps only location and boundary tracking, and language options.

improve.needs: What Dami would change looking back, in her own words.

story.intro: LOCIT was our senior capstone at Kennesaw State: a GPS necklace and companion app that lets a family see where a loved one is, and get an alert if they leave a safe zone. The name stands for Location Integrated Tracker, and it’s a pun on “locket”, since the tracker is worn as a pendant. I led our four-person team, AZAD, from design through testing, and wrote the product requirements.
meta: Python, C, Raspberry Pi, AWS IoT, FlutterFlow, Figma, Fusion 360

sections.label: problem
sections.headline: Tracking that still needs a phone
paras: Families with young kids or elderly relatives want to know where their people are. The trackers everyone knows, Apple AirTag and Tile, depend on a phone, and the people we were designing for often don’t carry one.
So the question became: what would a tracker look like if the wearer didn’t need a phone at all?

sections.label: goal
sections.headline: Light enough to forget you’re wearing it
paras: I wrote the requirements with measurable targets, so we could test the prototype against them instead of guessing:
after: We also set a 24-hour battery life target, and room for up to three trackers on one phone.

sections.label: challenge
sections.headline: Everything had to fit in a pendant
paras: Our first 3D-printed enclosure was too bulky to wear as a necklace. We kept shrinking and reprinting it until the GPS module, microcontroller and battery fit.
We also had to cut scope. UV sensors came out because the parts took too long to arrive, Bluetooth came in, and we revised the requirements to match what we could actually build.

figures.alt: Hand sketch of the LOCIT necklace pendant: a round case on a cord, with the circuit board, wiring and modules drawn inside it in red.
figures.caption: Early concept sketch: what had to fit inside the pendant.

sections.label: process
sections.headline: Three decisions that shaped it

steps.title: A pendant, not a band
steps.text: We compared an armband, a brooch and a sling bag. The pendant won: discreet, comfortable, and close to where a forward-facing camera would need to sit.

steps.title: Take the data off the app
steps.text: FlutterFlow couldn’t keep up with real-time data coming straight from AWS. We moved it onto a web server: the necklace uploads, the server stores, the app fetches. Sensor data transfer got about 20% faster.

steps.title: Tune the geofence to the GPS
steps.text: GPS accuracy decided how precisely we could catch a boundary crossing, so we refined the geofencing thresholds around it.

after: The companion app, built in FlutterFlow, shows live location, sets safe zones, and sends boundary, temperature and low-battery alerts. I modeled the enclosure in Fusion 360 and we printed it in PLA.

paras: The list we left ourselves: 24-hour battery life on a single charge, more thorough testing, a more polished app, and testing with real families.

exhibits.title: News Corp Product Strategy
exhibits.category: Product Management · User Research · AI Strategy
exhibits.teaser: AI Product Manager Intern, Aug to Oct 2025. How news sites personalize with AI, compared with TikTok and Spotify, and three feature proposals.

idea.text: Studied how news sites personalize content with AI, and compared them with TikTok and Spotify to recommend how news could feel more personal.
idea.src: Mini case scan; From User to Product Thinker

who.text: News Corp, during her AI Product Manager internship (August to October 2025).

how.text: Hands-on case scans of NY Post and BBC, browsing to see how quickly each changed what it showed, then a side-by-side comparison with TikTok and Spotify.
how.src: Mini case scan; From User to Product Thinker

items.text: How well do news sites personalize compared with the social and streaming apps people use every day?

why.needs: Why this mattered to News Corp’s digital teams.

items.text: Analyzed 500+ survey responses and developed five audience personas from reader preferences and trust concerns, then compared content discovery and personalization across four platforms and presented the findings.

NY Post: the homepage shifted from politics to entertainment after a few entertainment clicks, with no obvious preference controls. “Trending Now” and the sidebar followed the last click. No chatbot found.

BBC: shifted more slowly, from politics to science and technology. “My News” exists but has to be found. Related-content boxes reflected browsing. The app’s News Briefs and voice summaries are likely algorithmic.
Comparison: TikTok’s For You page personalizes most strongly, Spotify is strong, and the news sites are far behind. NY Post’s autoplay video and intrusive ads were the biggest friction.

Her reflection: she had not realized how quickly news sites change what they show after a few clicks, and even with AI personalization it felt less personal than social media. (Paraphrased; a direct quote needs the source PDF.)
Recommendations for news: make it feel personal, mix in discovery such as weekly roundups or topic playlists, and think mobile-first with quick, swipeable video.
Proposed three features: personalized feeds, weekly topic roundups and short-form video.
Projected improvements in content relevance and retention. These are recommendations and projections, not shipped outcomes.

results.needs: Survey data and how projections were estimated.
